title: Boiled Eggs with Soldiers
subtitle: Soft-boiled eggs and crisp buttered toast fingers
excerpt: Soft-boiled eggs with fingers of buttered toast for dipping, one of the most satisfying breakfasts in the British repertoire, and one children and adults eat with equal enthusiasm.
sourceNotes: A British breakfast tradition. The term 'soldiers' for toast fingers dipped in a soft egg appears in British usage from at least the mid-twentieth century.

glossaryTerms.definition: To maintain liquid at a temperature just below boiling, with small steady bubbles rather than a vigorous rolling boil.
Fingers of toast cut from a slice of bread, traditionally served upright alongside a soft-boiled egg for dipping into the yolk.

content.text: Boiled eggs with
soldiers

is one of the simplest, most reliably comforting breakfasts in the British kitchen, and the only version worth making is with a yolk that runs freely when you dip the first soldier in. The bread matters here: a thick slice of white sandwich bread or a good sourdough gives you a soldier with enough structure to reach the yolk without collapsing. Thin, flimsy toast is frustrating to eat and disrespects the egg.
What you need
You will also need 4 thick slices of bread, white sandwich loaf, sourdough, or wholemeal all work well.
Bring a saucepan of water to a rolling boil. Lower the eggs in gently with a slotted spoon. Start the timer immediately.
Cook for 5 minutes for a fully runny yolk or 6 minutes for a jammy centre. Toast and butter the bread while the eggs cook, then cut each slice into four fingers.
Lift the eggs out with the slotted spoon, set in egg cups, season the yolk with sea salt, and serve the soldiers alongside.
Boil the eggs
Fill the saucepan with enough water to submerge the
eggs
by 2 cm and bring it to a rolling boil. Lower the eggs in with the slotted spoon, gently, not dropped. Start your timer. Reduce to a steady
simmer
and cook for 5 minutes for a fully runny yolk, or 6 minutes for a yolk that is jammy and just starting to thicken at the edges.
Make the soldiers

Start the toast at the same time as the eggs, the idea is for both to be ready at the same moment. Toast the bread until golden and crisp, but stop before it colours too darkly or it will be too brittle for dipping. Butter the toast generously with the
unsalted-butter

while it is hot, so the butter melts in rather than sitting on the surface. Cut each slice into four fingers, not diagonal triangles, but straight-cut strips the full length of the bread. These are the soldiers.
Serve immediately

Lift the eggs with the slotted spoon and set each one in an egg cup. Place 2 eggs per person, with the soldiers arranged alongside. Tap the top of each egg firmly with a teaspoon, peel away the cap, and season the exposed yolk with a pinch of sea salt. Dip a soldier straight in. If you leave the eggs in the shells for more than a minute or two they continue to cook from residual heat, so eat them quickly.
Troubleshooter

Yolk has set by the time you get to the second egg: the eggs were left in the hot shell too long, or were at room temperature rather than fridge-cold. Get the egg cup and salt ready before the eggs come out of the water.

Soldiers go floppy: the bread is too thin or too soft. A medium-sliced sandwich loaf will flop into the yolk; a thick-cut slice or a slice of sourdough holds its shape. Cut the soldiers slightly wider than you think, a centimetre width is about right.
Where this dish lives

Boiled eggs and soldiers is a childhood staple across Britain, the breakfast that most adults remember from Saturday mornings or holidays with grandparents. The egg cup is such a distinctly British piece of kitchen equipment that it barely needs explaining here. The dish appears in school stories, in wartime recipe pamphlets, and on the breakfast menus of country house hotels. It is quick, warming, and one of those meals that feels like an act of kindness to make for someone.
